notes: Ruling slot 3 = Congress (R) of Indira Gandhi after the November 1969 split; Congress (O) takes slot 1. Swatantra moved from MD slot 16 to slot 2 so the largest opposition party of 1967 keeps starting popularity (MD sprite reused, same party); the Forum of Free Enterprise fills 16. Coalition slot 18 holds the SSP as the natural non-aligned socialist party, although Indira's minority government actually rested on outside support from the CPI (slot 4), the DMK (slot 20) and the Akali Dal. DMK sits in 20 as the Dravidian nationalist-populist party because 14 (Jana Sangh) and 18 (SSP) were the only fitting popular slots. No free fitting slot remained for the PSP and the Shiromani Akali Dal. CPI(ML) (April 1969) is in 5, CPI(M) follows MD in 19.

0.name: Concord of Princes
0.text:
The Concord of Princes is the association through which India's former ruling maharajas, nawabs and rajas defend the privy purses and privileges guaranteed to them when their states acceded to the Union in 1947-49. Formed in 1967 when the abolition of the purses first came onto the Congress agenda, it now faces a Prime Minister who has made their removal a symbol of her left turn.

The princes stand for property, hereditary dignity, the sanctity of the accession covenants and a Western-leaning, anti-socialist India. Several of them sit in parliament for the Swatantra Party or as independents, among them Gayatri Devi of Jaipur and Karni Singh of Bikaner. Their leverage lies in great wealth, rural patronage and the loyalty that former subjects still show their royal houses.

1.name: Indian National Congress (Organisation)
1.text:
Congress (O) is the old guard of the ruling party, the bosses of the 'Syndicate' who expelled Indira Gandhi in November 1969 and lost most of the parliamentary party to her. Party president S. Nijalingappa, Morarji Desai, K. Kamaraj, S. K. Patil and Atulya Ghosh lead some sixty-five Lok Sabha members and still govern Gujarat and Mysore.

The Organisation Congress presents itself as the guardian of Gandhian values, constitutional propriety and sound finance against what it calls Indira's opportunist populism and her dependence on communist votes. It defends private enterprise, distrusts bank nationalisation and leans towards the West. Its strength is the network of state party machines, business donors and rural notables built over two decades of Congress rule.

2.name: Swatantra Party
2.text:
C. Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party in 1959 in protest against Nehru's planned economy and the threat of cooperative farming. With N. G. Ranga, Minoo Masani and Piloo Mody it won forty-four seats in 1967, becoming the largest opposition party in the Lok Sabha, and it heads the coalition government of Orissa.

Swatantra calls for the dismantling of the 'licence-permit raj', the protection of property, an end to bank nationalisation and the abolition of compulsory procurement. Abroad it wants close ties with the United States and the West instead of Soviet friendship. Its unusual coalition of industrialists, former princes and landowning peasants in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Orissa and Andhra gives it money and rural reach.

3.name: Indian National Congress (R)
3.text:
Founded in 1885 and the party of Gandhi and Nehru, the Indian National Congress split in November 1969 when the old bosses expelled Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Her Congress (R), with Jagjivan Ram elected president at its Bombay session in December, keeps the government but has lost its majority and survives with the votes of the CPI, the DMK and the Akali Dal.

Indira has staked her future on a turn to the left: the nationalisation of fourteen banks in July 1969, the election of V. V. Giri as President against the party machine, and the promised abolition of the princes' privy purses. Her Congress stands for planning, secularism and non-alignment with a growing tilt towards Moscow, and appeals to the poor, Dalits, Muslims and the young.

4.name: Communist Party of India
4.text:
Founded in 1925, the Communist Party of India lost much of its cadre in the 1964 split but remains Moscow's party in India under General Secretary C. Rajeswara Rao and Chairman S. A. Dange. It holds twenty-three seats in the Lok Sabha, and since November 1969 its C. Achutha Menon heads a coalition government in Kerala.

The CPI follows the Soviet line of 'national democracy', backing the 'progressive' Congress against monopoly capital, feudal princes and imperialism. It supports Indira Gandhi's minority government from outside and hails bank nationalisation as a first step. Its strength lies in the AITUC trade unions, the peasant leagues of Andhra and Kerala, and its influence among intellectuals and Congress radicals.

5.name: Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist)
5.text:
The CPI(ML) was founded in Calcutta on 22 April 1969 by revolutionaries expelled from the CPI(M) after the peasant rising at Naxalbari in 1967, which Beijing hailed as 'spring thunder over India'. Charu Majumdar is its leader and theoretician, Kanu Sanyal its best-known organiser, and the party works entirely underground.

The Naxalites reject elections as a fraud and call for protracted people's war on the Chinese model, encircling the cities from the countryside. Majumdar's line of 'annihilation of class enemies' sends small squads against landlords and moneylenders in Srikakulam, Debra-Gopiballavpur and Mushahari. Its recruits are tribal sharecroppers and the brightest students of Calcutta's colleges, and it treats Moscow and the parliamentary left alike as revisionist.

6.name: All India Forward Bloc
6.text:
Subhas Chandra Bose created the Forward Bloc in 1939 as a militant wing inside Congress, and it survived his death as an independent party keeping alive the cult of Netaji and the Indian National Army. Led by veterans such as Hemanta Kumar Basu, it sits in the United Front government of West Bengal and has pockets of strength in southern Tamil Nadu.

The Bloc marries Bose's martial, disciplined nationalism to a Marxist programme of nationalisation, land reform and planning. It is fiercely anti-imperialist, distrusts the Western powers and looks to the Soviet bloc as the natural partner of a strong India. Its leverage comes from its place in the Bengal left alliance and the emotional pull of Netaji's legend.

7.name: Research and Analysis Wing
7.text:
India's foreign intelligence service was carved out of the Intelligence Bureau in September 1968 after the failures of the wars of 1962 and 1965. Under its founding chief Rameshwar Nath Kao it answers directly to Indira Gandhi and her secretariat and is quickly building networks in Pakistan, East Bengal, Tibet and the Himalayan kingdoms.

The 'Kaoboys' are a secret state within the state, trusted by the Prime Minister and free of parliamentary scrutiny. They see American arms for Pakistan and Chinese support for Naga, Mizo and Naxalite rebels as the main threats and value the Soviet connection as India's insurance. Their influence rests on privileged access to the Prime Minister and on covert means no other institution commands.

8.name: All India Shia Conference
8.text:
The All India Shia Conference was founded at Lucknow in 1907 to speak for the Shia minority within Indian Islam. Rooted in the old aristocracy of Awadh, the imambaras of Lucknow and the trading communities of Bombay and Hyderabad, it opposed the Muslim League and partition and has remained loyal to Congress since independence.

The Conference asks for the protection of Shia endowments, the right to hold Muharram processions undisturbed, Shia representation in waqf boards and fair treatment in Sunni-dominated Muslim bodies. It seeks reform through education and lobbying, not agitation. Its weight lies in the respect commanded by Lucknow's Shia families and in the votes of compact Shia communities in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Kashmir.

9.name: Anjuman-e-Sharie Shian
9.text:
The Anjuman-e-Sharie Shian is the religious and political organisation of the Shia of Kashmir, founded and led by Aga Syed Yusuf al-Moosavi al-Safavi of Budgam. The Aga presides over a dense network of mosques, imambaras and schools in the Kashmir valley.

The Anjuman collects khums and fitra from the faithful and administers them for education and relief, giving its clergy an independent financial base. It insists that the law of the Shia community must be decided by qualified jurists rather than the secular state, and it has already forced Srinagar to exempt Shias from rules it judged contrary to Islamic law. Its leverage is the discipline of a congregation that follows its marja and its Aga.

10.name: Markazi Jamiat Ahl-e-Hadith Hind
10.english: Central Society of Ahl-e-Hadith of India
10.text:
The Ahl-e-Hadith movement has organised itself since the founding of the All-India Ahl-e-Hadith Conference in 1906, in which Maulana Sanaullah Amritsari played a leading role. Its central body runs mosques, madrasas and publishing houses across north India, from Delhi and Benares to Bihar and Bengal, and keeps ties with the scholars of Saudi Arabia.

The movement teaches a return to the Quran and the authentic hadith, rejecting the imitation of the law schools, saint worship and Sufi shrine cults. Politically it is quietist and loyal to the Indian state, seeing personal piety and correct belief rather than agitation as the path for Muslims. Its influence lies in its preachers, its schools and growing links with Saudi charities.

11.name: Jamaat-e-Islami Hind
11.text:
Jamaat-e-Islami Hind was formed in 1948 by the members of Maulana Maududi's movement who stayed in India after partition. Led by its Amir, Maulana Abul Lais Islahi Nadvi, from its headquarters in Delhi, it is a tightly selected cadre organisation with study circles, schools and publishing houses.

The Jamaat's goal is 'iqamat-e-deen', the establishment of God's sovereignty over every sphere of life, and it regards secular democracy and nationalism as idols to be overcome. It keeps its members out of electoral politics and works for an Islamic revolution of minds rather than of arms. Its influence rests on educated, devout young Muslims who see the Muslim League and the ulama as compromised by the Indian state.

12.name: Indian Union Muslim League
12.text:
The Indian Union Muslim League was constituted at Madras in 1948 from the part of Jinnah's Muslim League that remained in India. Under its president Muhammed Ismail, the 'Quaid-e-Millat', it is strongest among the Mappila Muslims of Malabar, and since November 1969 its ministers, led by C. H. Mohammed Koya, sit in Kerala's coalition government.

The League defends Muslim personal law, Urdu and Arabic education, minority institutions and reservations for backward Muslims, while accepting the secular constitution. It is a pragmatic coalition partner that has worked with communists and Congress alike, and it lobbied for the Muslim-majority district of Malappuram, created in June 1969. Its leverage is the disciplined Muslim vote of northern Kerala.

13.name: Prime Minister's Secretariat
13.text:
Since 1967 the Prime Minister's Secretariat under P. N. Haksar has grown from a small office into the nerve centre of Indian government. Haksar, a former diplomat and Nehruvian of the left, drafted the bank nationalisation and guided Indira Gandhi through the Congress split, and with a circle of Kashmiri officials and economists he shapes policy far beyond the reach of ministers.

The Secretariat believes in a 'committed bureaucracy' that serves the Prime Minister's socialist programme rather than neutral procedure. It centralises economic planning, appointments and intelligence in Delhi and treats state governments and party bosses as obstacles. Its power is that of proximity: it controls the files, the agenda and access to the most powerful person in India.

14.name: Bharatiya Jana Sangh
14.text:
The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was founded in 1951 by Syama Prasad Mookerjee with the backing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. After the mysterious death of Deendayal Upadhyaya in 1968 it is led by Atal Bihari Vajpayee, with L. K. Advani and Balraj Madhok as prominent figures. It holds thirty-five Lok Sabha seats and has shared power in several coalition state governments since 1967.

The Jana Sangh preaches 'Integral Humanism', cultural nationalism and the 'Indianisation' of public life, with Hindi, cow protection and a firm line against Pakistan and China. It opposes bank nationalisation and calls for an Indian nuclear deterrent. Its base is the Hindu trading classes and refugees of the north, and its cadres come from the disciplined shakhas of the RSS.

15.name: Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry
15.english: Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry
15.text:
FICCI was founded in 1927 by G. D. Birla and Purshottamdas Thakurdas as the voice of Indian capital in the national movement. Today it speaks for the great business houses, the Birlas, Tatas, Singhanias and Dalmias, which the Monopolies Inquiry Commission found to control a large share of private industry.

The Federation is on the defensive. The nationalisation of the banks in July 1969 cut off the houses' easy credit, and the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act passed in December now threatens their expansion. FICCI lobbies for relaxed licensing, protection from foreign competition and tax relief, and quietly funds Congress (O) and the Swatantra Party. Its leverage is money, managerial talent and the dependence of planned industry on private capital.
15.wiki: Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industry

16.name: Forum of Free Enterprise
16.text:
The Forum of Free Enterprise was founded in Bombay in 1956 by the banker A. D. Shroff, one of the authors of the 1944 Bombay Plan, to argue the case for markets against Nehru's planned economy. Though non-partisan, it shares men and ideas with the Swatantra Party and with Minoo Masani's anti-communist circles.

The Forum publishes booklets, organises lectures and essay competitions in colleges and briefs journalists on the costs of controls, state monopolies and confiscatory taxation. It opposes bank nationalisation, price controls and the licensing system, and praises the export-led growth of Japan and Taiwan. Its influence lies in Bombay's business community, the English-language press and the educated middle class.

17.name: Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh
17.text:
The Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh was founded in 1964 at Gopeshwar in the Garhwal Himalaya by Chandi Prasad Bhatt and fellow Sarvodaya workers. It organises labour cooperatives and small village industries based on forest products in the Alaknanda valley.

The Sangh believes the hill villages must control the forests on which they live, and it resents a Forest Department that auctions oak, ash and pine to contractors from the plains while denying locals timber for ploughs and houses. It preaches Gandhian self-reliance, the protection of slopes against erosion and landslides, and the participation of village women. Its strength is moral rather than numerical: the respect of hill communities and its links to Vinoba Bhave's Sarvodaya movement.

18.name: Samyukta Socialist Party
18.text:
The Samyukta Socialist Party carries on the legacy of Ram Manohar Lohia, who died in 1967. With twenty-three Lok Sabha seats and leaders such as Madhu Limaye, George Fernandes, Raj Narain and Karpoori Thakur, it is the more radical of India's two socialist parties and has shared power in the non-Congress coalition governments of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

The SSP preaches 'non-Congressism', reserved places for the backward castes, Hindi in place of English, and a decentralised socialism of small machines and land to the tiller. It is equally distant from Washington and Moscow and suspicious of Indira's sudden radicalism. Its base lies among the Yadav and Kurmi peasants of the Gangetic plain and the trade unions of Bombay.

19.name: Communist Party of India (Marxist)
19.text:
The CPI(M) broke away from the CPI in 1964, rejecting cooperation with Congress. Under General Secretary P. Sundarayya and E. M. S. Namboodiripad, it is now the strongest communist party in India: Jyoti Basu is Deputy Chief Minister of West Bengal's United Front government, while Namboodiripad's Kerala ministry fell only in October 1969.

The party keeps its distance from both Moscow and Beijing, which denounced it as revisionist after Naxalbari. It combines parliamentary work with militant mass struggle, land occupations and gheraos of factory managers, and fights the Naxalites for the loyalty of the left. Its base is the industrial workers, sharecroppers and refugees of Bengal and the agricultural labourers of Kerala.

20.name: Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam
20.text:
C. N. Annadurai founded the DMK in 1949 after breaking with Periyar's Dravidar Kazhagam, and in 1967 it swept the Congress from power in Madras, which it renamed Tamil Nadu. After Annadurai's death in February 1969, M. Karunanidhi became Chief Minister, while film star M. G. Ramachandran draws the crowds. Its twenty-five MPs help keep Indira Gandhi's minority government alive.

The DMK is the party of Tamil pride: born in the agitations against the imposition of Hindi, it champions the Tamil language, the dignity of the non-Brahmin castes and far-reaching autonomy for the states, now being studied by its Rajamannar Committee. It wins votes with cheap rice and cinema glamour and organises through a dense network of party clubs and reading rooms.

21.name: Shiv Sena
21.text:
Bal Thackeray, a cartoonist whose weekly Marmik railed against south Indian clerks in Bombay's offices, founded the Shiv Sena in June 1966. Organised in neighbourhood branches of young Marathi men, it won a bloc of seats on the Bombay Municipal Corporation in 1968, and in February 1969 its agitation over the Belgaum border dispute ended in days of rioting and Thackeray's arrest.

The Sena demands jobs and housing for the 'sons of the soil' and attacks migrants, communists and trade unions with street violence. Thackeray openly admires strong leaders and scorns parliamentary politics. Bombay industrialists and some Congress politicians quietly use the Sena to break the communist unions, which gives it protection, funds and a growing following in the mill districts.

22.name: Indian Armed Forces
22.text:
With well over a million men, the Indian Armed Forces are among the largest in the world, and unlike their counterparts in Pakistan and Burma they have stayed under civilian control since independence. Humiliated by China in 1962 and fought to a draw by Pakistan in 1965, the army has been rebuilt with Soviet and domestic arms and is led since June 1969 by General Sam Manekshaw.

The officer corps prizes its apolitical tradition, but its weight is growing: it fights Naga and Mizo insurgents in the north-east, guards the Himalayan frontier and watches the unrest in East Pakistan. Its influence comes from the defence budget, the prestige of the services and the dependence of every government on their loyalty.

23.name: Akhil Bharat Hindu Mahasabha
23.text:
Founded in 1915, the Hindu Mahasabha was the party of V. D. Savarkar, who coined the doctrine of Hindutva and died in 1966. Discredited by the assassination of Gandhi by a former member in 1948 and overshadowed by the Jana Sangh, it survives as a small party, strongest around the Gorakhnath Math of Gorakhpur, whose Mahant Digvijay Nath held a Lok Sabha seat until his death in 1969.

The Mahasabha calls for a Hindu Rashtra, the reunification of partitioned India and the militarisation of Hindu society. It reveres the King of Nepal as the world's only Hindu sovereign, defends the princely houses against abolition of their privy purses and rejects secularism as appeasement. Its influence lies in temples, monasteries and a loyal orthodox following.
